newsitem.title: MALI: Mali signals pro-American shift on top U.N. job.
newsitem.headline: Mali signals pro-American shift on top U.N. job.

text.p: Mali signalled on Tuesday it could accept a U.S. veto of the renomination of Boutros Boutros-Ghali for a new term as U.N. secretary-general provided the job went to another African.
Foreign Minister Dioncounda Traore stated Mali's position after talks between U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Malian President Alpha Oumar Konare
"Officially, what I could say now is that he (Boutros-Ghali) remains Africa's candidate," the minister told a joint news conference, before adding:
"I must stress the essential point for us is that Africa have a second mandate as the head of the U.N. This is really the most important issue for all African countries."
Mali had previously voiced unequivocal backing for the 73-year-old Egyptian, dismissed by the United States as unfit to lead the world body into the 21st century.

Mali's redefined position appears more in line with that of the Organisation of African Unity which officially backs Boutros-Ghali while holding the door open for another candidate should Washington make good its veto threat. Some countries like Niger, have already made known their candidates in waiting.
The issue of the U.N. job is at the top of the agenda of Christopher's five-nation Africa tour, the first by a U.S. secretary of state to the region for more than six years.

Another diplomatic topic is how to pressure Nigeria's ruling generals to speed the country's transition to democracy. Christopher said as he headed for Mali on Monday that he would seek a consesus for further sanctions against the Nigerian government, on top of limited ones imposed by the West.

Nigeria angered the international community by hanging nine minority activists last November in defiance of appeals for clemency. The military government was already under censure for aborting democratic elections in June 1993.
Christopher pointedly left out the regional giant from his circuit, starting his tour in impoverished Mali as a tribute to its own smooth change from one-party dictatorship to democracy.
At the news conferenmce, also attended by Christopher and Konare, Traore made an impassioned plea for Africa's right to a second tenure of the top U.N job.

"Please trust Africans. We have the means to contribute to the U.N. How can you the international community trust us with your confidence? By giving us a second term as head of the U.N. This is really what is essential to us," he said.

Christopher spelt out his diplomatic strategy to reporters on his plane on Monday: "Everywhere I go, I'm going to be talking about the importance of Africa coming forward with good candidates for the U.N. secretary generalship."

U.S. officials said they believed Malian leaders heard the U.S. message and were persuaded the U.N. post could be lost to Africa if they did not drop Boutros-Ghali, whose term runs out at the end of December.
Washington insists Boutros-Ghali must be replaced with a more reform-minded secretary general who can cut waste and prepare the U.N. for greater challenges.

Christopher announced that U.S. Peace Corps volunteers would soon begin returning to northern Mali because of Konare's success in ending ethnic conflict in that region. He announced a $1 million U.S. aid package to help demilitarise and retrain Tuareg rebels in the region and $700,000 to help Mali prepare for its second democratic election in 1997.
Christopher's schedule includes visits to Ethiopia, Tanzania, South Africa and Angola.
